data.text/markdown:
Can any model beat the naive baselines?

Real benchmark for half-hourly energy data is seasonal naive (same slot yesterday = lag 48, same slot last week = lag 336), not plain naive. A model only earns its place if it captures something those miss without adding estimation noise. This notebook runs the checklist on the 15 assets in src/data/metering_data.parquet (EV chargers + solar/battery, 14 days):
  1. Baselines first (statsforecast): Naive, SeasonalNaive(48), SeasonalNaive(336), seasonal window average, AutoETS.
  2. LightGBM (mlforecast) with only day-ahead-safe lags (>= 48), raw vs. Differences([48]) target.
  3. Ensembles.
  4. Rolling-origin cross_validation with several windows, scored with MASE (scale-free), per-asset win rate, and error by horizon.
Day-ahead framing: forecast 48 slots at 00:00 from data up to the previous midnight (h=48).

1. Baselines (statsforecast)

Naive is flat for 48 steps, so it is a weak benchmark at day-ahead. The two seasonal naives carry the daily and weekly shape for free. With only 14 days, AutoETS(season_length=48) has very little to learn from.

data.text/markdown:
2. LightGBM (mlforecast)

Two things matter here:
  • Lags >= 48 only. A lag-1 feature would force recursive prediction and let errors compound across the day. With lags 48/96/144 plus a rolling mean on lag 48, one predict(h=48) is valid and nothing leaks. (Lag 336 is left out: with 14 days it would delete most training rows. 336 stays a baseline.)
  • Target transform. Differences([48]) makes the model predict the deviation from seasonal naive, so it cannot lose the level. Compare it with the raw target, and with an extra LocalStandardScaler. Trees cannot extrapolate, so on level-shifting series the differenced version is the safer bet. On a stable series like this, the raw one may win. Look at the numbers rather than assume.
static_features=["is_solar"] tells the single global model which assets are solar.

data.text/markdown:
3. Ensembles

Equal-weight means. An ensemble only helps if its members are individually reasonable. The first is the generic "ETS + seasonal naive + LGBM" recipe, the second uses the members that actually did well on this data (picked on the same backtest, so treat it as optimistic).

data.text/html:
4. Scores (mean over 15 assets)

MASE < 1 means better than in-sample seasonal naive(48). Skill = 1 - MAE / MAE_reference (positive = better). "Best baseline" is the hardest of the five baselines, which is the bar that counts.

5. Per-asset win rate

Share of the 15 assets where the model has lower MAE than the baseline. A model that wins on most assets but loses badly on a few is still useful. "worst asset ratio" shows how bad the bad ones are (above 1.00x = worse than SN48).

6. MASE by asset type

Aggregates hide structure: EV charging and solar+battery respond differently to each model.

data.text/markdown:
Verdict

Yes. Hardest baseline is SN336 (MAE 0.236). LGB_raw beats it with MAE 0.185 (21.5% skill). Caveats: 14 days gives only a few backtest windows, so differences of a few percent are within noise. The winner was picked on the same windows it is scored on. Re-check as more history arrives. Extra data (calendar, tariff signals, weather) is the other lever, since without a real information advantage the model has the baseline's information plus parameters to fit.
